title: Seminar: The Ethics of Gene Editing

transcript.speaker: S1
transcript.text: For our ethics seminar, let's tackle gene editing. In 2018, a scientist in China announced the birth of twins whose genes had been edited as embryos to resist HIV. Tom, what was the reaction?

transcript.speaker: S2
transcript.text: Condemnation, almost universally. He was criticised for acting before safety had been demonstrated, and for inadequate consent from the parents. He was later sentenced to three years in prison.

transcript.speaker: S1
transcript.text: But the ethical question goes beyond that one case. Nadia, what's the central issue?

transcript.speaker: S3
transcript.text: I'd distinguish between editing somatic cells, which affects only the patient, and editing germline cells, which are passed on to future generations. Somatic therapies, like the recent treatments for sickle cell disease, are widely accepted because they resemble other medical treatments. The germline is controversial because the people affected can't consent.

transcript.speaker: S2
transcript.text: Although you could argue that parents make decisions for unborn children all the time.

transcript.speaker: S3
transcript.text: True, but the decisions here are irreversible, and might have unforeseen effects across generations. And there's a difference between decisions about a particular child's upbringing and permanent changes to the human gene pool.

transcript.speaker: S1
transcript.text: Let's examine the distinction between therapy and enhancement. Tom?

transcript.speaker: S2
transcript.text: I'm sceptical that the line is clear. If we can prevent a disease, why not prevent a predisposition to disease? And if that's acceptable, what about increasing resistance to infection beyond normal levels? Each step looks like a modest extension of the previous one.

transcript.speaker: S3
transcript.text: This is the slippery slope argument, which philosophers are wary of, because it can be used to resist any change. But in this case I think the concern is legitimate, since commercial pressure would push towards enhancement for those who can pay.

transcript.speaker: S1
transcript.text: Which raises the issue of justice.

transcript.speaker: S3
transcript.text: Exactly. If only wealthy families can afford enhancement, existing inequalities could become biological. It's one thing for rich children to attend better schools; it's another for them to be, in some measure, genetically advantaged.

transcript.speaker: S2
transcript.text: Yet one could respond that this applies to all technologies at first. Mobile phones were once luxuries.

transcript.speaker: S1
transcript.text: The analogy has limits. A phone can be given to everyone later. A genetic change in earlier generations can't be made available to those already born.

transcript.speaker: S3
transcript.text: There's also the point that we understand genes much less well than the popular image suggests. Most traits, such as intelligence, involve thousands of genes, each with a tiny effect, and the same gene may influence several traits. So editing for one outcome might have unexpected consequences.

transcript.speaker: S2
transcript.text: I accept that, and it argues for caution, rather than prohibition. A moratorium, for example, rather than a permanent ban.

transcript.speaker: S1
transcript.text: Many scientists have called for just that, together with international regulation. The difficulty is enforcement: a country with lax rules could attract genetic tourism.

transcript.speaker: S2
transcript.text: Which suggests the debate needs to be global rather than national.

transcript.speaker: S1
transcript.text: For your essay, take a position on whether germline editing should ever be permitted, and anticipate the strongest objection to your view.
